steps.title: Key idea 1
steps.body: Chromatography is a separation technique used to separate the components of a mixture. It works because different substances have different solubilities in the same solvent, so they travel at different rates through the stationary phase.

steps.title: Key idea 2
steps.body: Chromatography has two phases: Mobile phase — the solvent that moves through the paper (e.g. water or ethanol). Stationary phase — the material that does not move (e.g. chromatography paper). Components that are more soluble in the mobile phase travel faster and further. Components that are more attracted to the stationary phase travel slower and stay closer to the origin.

steps.title: Key idea 3
steps.body: Follow these steps to carry out paper chromatography: Draw a pencil baseline near the bottom of the chromatography paper. Never use ink — it would dissolve and run. Place small spots of each sample on the baseline using a capillary tube. Place the paper in a beaker containing a small amount of solvent . The solvent level must be below the baseline. Cover the beaker with a lid to prevent evaporation and keep the atmosphere saturated with solvent vapour. Allow the solvent to rise up the paper by capillary action . When the solvent nears the top, remove the paper and mark the solvent front with a pencil. Allow the paper to dry. If spots are colourless, use a locating agent or UV light to make them visible.

steps.title: Key idea 4
steps.body: The result is a chromatogram — a pattern of spots showing where each component has moved to on the paper.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: When interpreting a chromatogram: A pure substance produces a single spot on the chromatogram. A mixture produces two or more spots , because the different components separate out. Two substances are likely the same compound if they produce spots at the same height (same Rf value) when run on the same chromatogram. If a spot from a known reference is at the same position as a spot from an unknown sample, the unknown likely contains that substance. Always measure to the centre of the spot when calculating Rf values, not the top or bottom edge.
